title: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although terrestrial mammals are absent from oceanic islands, bats occur on almost every island, and remote islands often have their own endemic bat species, because bats can fly across wide spaces of sea and are then modified in their new homes.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Though terrestrial mammals do not occur on oceanic islands, ærial mammals do occur on almost every island.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals”. Scope: bats on oceanic islands

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-10: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.91

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern global mammal ranges and island inventories directly test both occupancy and endemicity. Survey completeness can be modeled, leaving high power to confirm or refute the broad pattern.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure bat occupancy and endemic-species proportions across a global set of islands as functions of isolation, area, and survey completeness, contrasting non-volant mammals. Support requires near-ubiquitous bat presence and elevated endemicity on remote islands.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Almost every island' needs an island-size and survey threshold.

Small remote islands are undersurveyed for bats.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Bat checklists for islands and archipelagos are public and can be joined to isolation distance. Presence on remote islands and the endemism of those bats are both countable, with a pre-set size cutoff to make almost every operational. Undersurvey of the smallest islets limits absence claims and does not block the test for islands large enough to have been searched.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score bat presence, and the fraction of bat species endemic to the island, across oceanic islands ordered by isolation. Absence of bats from most remote islands, or no rise in endemism with isolation, would count against the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Almost every island needs a minimum size, because tiny islets are poor bat habitat.

Endemism depends on whether island populations are ranked as species.

Small islands are poorly surveyed for bats, so absence is weaker evidence than presence.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If Darwin is right, bats are recorded on almost every remote oceanic island group that has been reasonably surveyed, and a substantial share of those groups have bat species found nowhere else, in sharp contrast with the near-absence of native non-volant land mammals on the same islands.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py reads the 43 far island units (> 482.8 km from any landmass >= 100,000 km2) and their GBIF filters from ../darwin1859-ch12-09/derived/units.json. For each unit it counts GBIF bird records (survey proxy, threshold 500), then facets Chiroptera records by speciesKey; for each bat species it fetches the global record count (georeferenced-only for bounding-box units, all records for country-code units) and flags endemism at >= 10 records and >= 95 % inside the unit. A surveyed unit has bats if any species has >= 5 records in it. The pre-registered rule compares the occupancy fraction (thresholds 0.80 / 0.50) and the fraction of bat-occupied units with an endemic bat (0.33 / 0.10). Sensitivities: any single record counts as presence; endemism at >= 80 %.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Using the 43 pre-registered island units lying > 300 statute miles from any landmass >= 100,000 km2 (the far units of darwin1859-ch12-09, same GBIF filters and representative points), a unit counts as 'surveyed' if GBIF holds >= 500 non-fossil, non-captive bird (class Aves) records for it. A surveyed unit 'has bats' if at least one Chiroptera species has >= 5 non-fossil, non-captive GBIF records inside the unit (single records are treated as possible vagrants). A bat species is 'endemic' to a unit if it has >= 10 records worldwide and >= 95 % of them inside the unit (same rule as ch12-09). Supports if >= 80 % of surveyed far units have bats AND >= 33 % of the surveyed far units with bats have >= 1 endemic bat species.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refutes if < 50 % of surveyed far units have bats, or if < 10 % of the bat-occupied surveyed units have an endemic bat species. Otherwise mixed. The contrast with non-volant mammals is reported descriptively: the number of far units with an endemic bat species is compared with the number having an endemic non-volant terrestrial mammal from the same GBIF endemism rule (1 of 43 in darwin1859-ch12-09).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of surveyed far island units (>= 500 GBIF bird records) with a bat species having >= 5 GBIF records

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: GBIF snapshot counts; endemism rule >= 10 records and >= 95 % inside unit; units are archipelago-level

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'almost every island' is read as 'almost every remote oceanic island group that naturalists have actually searched', since he was generalising from the islands then known; the Aves-record threshold is a proxy for survey effort independent of bats. 'Their own species' is operationalised as GBIF endemism at the unit level; subspecies-level endemics (e.g. the Hawaiian hoary bat, treated by GBIF as Lasiurus cinereus or Aeorestes semotus depending on the backbone) are counted only if the backbone treats them as species. 'Remote' uses the ch12-09 distance rule (> 482.8 km from any landmass >= 100,000 km2), so the test is on the same 43 units for which the absence of terrestrial mammals was tested. Units are archipelago-level (country codes or bounding boxes), so a bat endemic to one island within a group counts as endemic to the unit. The threshold of >= 5 records per species is intended to exclude storm-blown vagrants (e.g. North American bats recorded in Iceland or Bermuda) while keeping genuinely resident but poorly recorded species; a sensitivity with >= 1 record is reported.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
GBIF occurrence search API (order Chiroptera, non-fossil, non-captive records), faceted by species per island unit

GBIF occurrence search API (class Aves, non-fossil, non-captive records), record count per island unit

GBIF species API (backbone taxonomy)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Occupancy: 25 of 40 surveyed far units (62.5 %) have a bat species with >= 5 records, between the supports (80 %) and refutes (50 %) thresholds; counting any single record gives 32 of 43 units (74 %). Bats are nearly universal on tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean archipelagos but absent from the remotest eastern Polynesian groups (French Polynesia, Pitcairn, Easter Island), from the South Atlantic islands (St Helena, Ascension, Tristan da Cunha, Falklands, South Georgia), from the subantarctic (Kerguelen) and from Iceland, so 'almost every island' is an overstatement for the most isolated islands Darwin did not know well.

Endemism: 5 of 25 bat-occupied units (20 %) have an endemic bat by the strict 95 % rule (Azores, Hawaii, Ogasawara, Reunion, Solomon Islands); 5 far units have an endemic bat versus 1 (Galapagos) with an endemic non-volant mammal in darwin1859-ch12-09, which is the contrast Darwin draws.

The 95 % endemism cut-off is too strict for country-code units: well-known single-archipelago endemics such as Pteropus ornatus (94.9 % of records in New Caledonia), Notopteris neocaledonicus (93.3 %), Pteropus anetianus (92.5 %, Vanuatu), Pteropus aldabrensis (89 %, Seychelles) and Mormopterus acetabulosus (85 %, Mauritius) fall just below it because some museum records lack a country code. At >= 80 % the count rises to 9 of 25 bat-occupied units (36 %) and 18 endemic species, which would satisfy the endemism half of the supports rule; the occupancy half would still fail.

Several Pacific units are undersurveyed for bats even above the bird threshold: Niue (0 bat records) and Wallis and Futuna (4 records) are both known to hold Pteropus tonganus; Norfolk Island's Chalinolobus gouldii (2 records) is a historical resident. Correcting these three would raise occupancy to 28 of 40 (70 %), still short of 80 %.

Bermuda's seven bat species (24 records) are all North American migrants or vagrants with no resident population; the >= 5 record rule nonetheless counts Bermuda as occupied, which inflates occupancy slightly in Darwin's favour.

Hawaii's endemic is counted via the GBIF backbone species Aeorestes semotus (Hawaiian hoary bat), which many authorities treat as a subspecies of the hoary bat; Darwin's 'their own species' is sensitive to such taxonomic rank decisions.

Units are archipelago-level (country codes or boxes), so 'island' here means island group; bat-free individual islands within occupied groups are not counted against the claim.
